title: API Gateway Patterns
summary: Centralizing auth, rate limiting, routing, and transformation at a single entry point in front of many services — and where that entry point stops being a good idea.

slides.markdown:
An **API gateway** sits in front of a set of backend services as the single entry point every client request passes through. Instead of every service reimplementing auth, rate limiting, and logging, the gateway does it once, centrally, then routes the request on to whichever service actually handles it.

Think of it as a building's front desk: visitors don't wander straight to any office — they check in once at the desk (auth, rate limiting), and the desk directs them to the right floor (routing). This topic covers what a gateway centralizes well, and the one common way teams misuse it.

slides.sectionTitle: What an API gateway centralizes: auth, rate limiting, routing, transformation
slides.markdown:
Without a gateway, every backend service has to independently implement authentication checks, rate limiting, request logging, and TLS termination — and independently gets it slightly wrong. A gateway centralizes all of it in one place: it validates a token or API key once, applies a rate limit per client, logs the request, and only then forwards it to the right service based on the path or hostname.

Routing is the most visible job — mapping `/orders/*` to the Orders service and `/users/*` to the Users service — but the value is really in the cross-cutting concerns every service would otherwise duplicate. A new service added behind the gateway inherits auth and rate limiting automatically, instead of the team having to reimplement both from scratch.

This is also where **transformation** happens: adapting an old client's request format to a newer backend's expected shape, or vice versa, without either side needing to change.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: gateway in front of many backend services
slides.markdown:
![API gateway routing authenticated traffic to five backend services](assets/gateway-fanout.svg)

Every request enters through one box. The gateway checks the token, enforces the rate limit, and then routes based on the path prefix — `/users/*` goes one way, `/payments/*` another. Each backend service only ever sees traffic that's already been authenticated and rate-limited; it doesn't duplicate that logic itself.

The services also don't need to know about each other — from any one service's point of view, all traffic just "arrives," already vetted.

slides.sectionTitle: Backend-for-frontend (BFF): a gateway per client type
slides.markdown:
A **backend-for-frontend (BFF)** is a variant where instead of one shared gateway for every client, each client type — mobile, web, a public partner API — gets its own dedicated gateway tuned to its exact needs. A mobile BFF might aggressively trim response payloads for slow connections; a web BFF might return richer, more detailed responses since bandwidth is less of a constraint.

This solves a real tension: a single shared gateway trying to serve every client's needs tends to accumulate client-specific conditional logic ("if mobile, trim these fields") that makes it fragile and hard to reason about. Splitting by client type lets each BFF evolve independently, on its own release schedule, without one client's change risking another's.

The cost is duplication — common logic (auth, for instance) now potentially lives in multiple BFFs unless it's factored into a shared layer underneath them.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: API gateway vs service mesh — where each one operates
slides.markdown:
| | API gateway | Service mesh |
|---|---|---|
| Traffic it handles | North-south — external clients into the system | East-west — service-to-service traffic inside the system |
| Typical concerns | Auth, rate limiting, routing, client-facing transformation | mTLS between services, retries, circuit breaking, internal observability |
| Where it lives | One (or a few) entry points at the edge | A sidecar proxy alongside every internal service instance |
| Client awareness | Client explicitly calls through it | Internal services often don't know it's there |

**How to decide:** these aren't competing choices — a gateway handles the edge, a mesh handles internal traffic between your own services, and many large systems run both. Reach for a mesh once service-to-service call volume and reliability needs (retries, mTLS, per-call observability) outgrow what application code should handle itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Request/response transformation and protocol translation at the gateway
slides.markdown:
Gateways commonly translate between what a client sends and what a backend actually expects — reshaping a JSON field, converting a public REST call into an internal gRPC call, or stripping internal-only fields before a response leaves the system. This lets backends evolve their internal contracts without forcing every external client to change in lockstep.

A common concrete case: a client on an old API version sends a field the backend has since renamed. The gateway maps the old field name to the new one on the way in, and maps the response back on the way out — the backend only ever sees its current contract, and the old client never notices anything changed.

This is powerful but has a limit, covered next: transformation logic can quietly grow into business logic if left unchecked.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: the gateway becoming a monolith of business logic
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The gateway already sits in front of everything, so it's the natural place to add this pricing rule / discount logic / user-tier check."

**Why it's wrong:** a gateway's job is cross-cutting infrastructure concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, transformation — that apply the same way regardless of what a request is *about*. Business logic (pricing, discounts, domain rules) is specific to a domain, changes on that domain's schedule, and belongs with the team that owns it. Once a gateway accumulates enough of this, it becomes a shared bottleneck: every domain team now has to coordinate deploys through the same central codebase, and a bug in one team's logic can take down routing for everyone.

**Correct model:** keep the gateway thin — auth, routing, rate limiting, generic transformation — and push anything that requires domain knowledge of a specific service back into that service, even if it means an extra hop.
